title: Nissan's in-factory AI cameras track employees to help worker safety
excerpt: Nissan is using AI cameras to track how factory workers move. They say it reduces injuries and cut health and safety costs.
content_html:
Nissan's in-factory AI cameras track how factory workers bend, walk, and build cars

By Ben Shimkus

You're currently following this author! Want to unfollow? Unsubscribe via the link in your email.

In Canton, Mississippi, where Nissan assembles the Altima sedan and the Frontier pickup, there are cameras watching how workers move.

The automaker says the AI-powered system is saving it millions of dollars — and ensuring that factory workers stay healthy.

"We're not talking about job elimination," Victor Taylor, Nissan's divisional vice president of manufacturing for the Americas, told Business Insider. "What we're referring to are mundane tasks that are really antiquated for a human being to be performing."

Nissan is the latest in a string of automobile companies highlighting how AI is changing the way Americans build cars, including improvements in initial quality and shorter development times.

But it is among the few willing to talk openly about how AI is watching its workers.

AI that fixes how workers bend and twist

Chi Amaechi, a Nissan process engineer and former safety engineer who worked on the system's implementation, said the Canton assembly plant has what it calls a "golden cycle" for each job.

The golden cycle represents the standard way a task should be performed, including the sequence for installing vehicle components, the time it should take, and body movements designed to reduce repetitive strain.

"What it does is it monitors body angles proactively," she said while showing Business Insider a virtual demonstration. "It's basically identifying your joints, so it can identify when a person is bending in a position that's beyond the safety requirement."

The system can detect when an employee bends too far or holds an unsafe position for too long, then flag the potential risk for factory managers. Supervisors and engineers can use that information to coach workers, reallocate tasks, or redesign a workstation.

Amaechi said the technology replaces time-consuming manual observations that can be inconsistent because employees may change their behavior when they know someone is watching.

According to Taylor, Nissan initially evaluated the technology to improve manufacturing efficiency and help train new workers. The ergonomic benefits emerged later.

"We weren't originally looking for that," he said of the safety applications. "It just kind of shown itself as, this is the biggest win."

The technology has also become part of Nissan's response to an aging workforce, Taylor said.

"We have employees that have been in the plant 20, 30-some odd years, and they want to retire," he added. "You can't replace 20, 30 years of know-how."

Taylor said employees were involved early through plant safety committees. He and Amaechi said workers initially worried that the technology could threaten jobs, but became more receptive when Nissan presented it as a safety and training tool. They also described instances in which workers welcomed changes made using the system.

Overall, Taylor said the technology has contributed to about $34 million in safety and health-related savings at Canton.

The system is deployed only in Canton. Taylor said Nissan plans to complete its rollout there before expanding it to the company's Smyrna, Tennessee, assembly plant and evaluating applications at its powertrain facilities.

A big turnaround

Nissan has had a rough few years, but it is showing early signs of a turnaround.

The automaker replaced Makoto Uchida with Ivan Espinosa as CEO in April 2025, shortly after Nissan and Honda abandoned merger talks. Espinosa subsequently introduced a recovery plan centered on cutting jobs, reducing manufacturing capacity, and streamlining Nissan's operations.

Canton's assembly line has been affected by some of those cuts: In May, the company canceled its $500 million plan to manufacture electric vehicles at the plant.

On Monday, Nissan reported its first quarterly net profit in two years, helped by cost reductions and stronger sales in the US and Japan. The automaker said its US sales rose nearly 10% during the quarter and called itself the fastest-growing mainstream brand over the previous 10 months.

The company calls itself America's "fastest-growing mainstream" car brand, per sales.

日产的工厂内人工智能摄像头跟踪工厂工人如何弯腰、行走和制造汽车

作者：Ben Shimkus 您目前正在关注该作者！ 想要取消关注吗？ 通过电子邮件中的链接取消订阅。

在密西西比州的坎顿，日产汽车组装 Altima 轿车和 Frontier 皮卡，那里有摄像头监视工人的行动。

该汽车制造商表示，人工智能驱动的系统为其节省了数百万美元，并确保工厂工人保持健康。

“我们不是在谈论裁员，”日产美洲制造部门副总裁维克多·泰勒 (Victor Taylor) 告诉《商业内幕》。 “我们指的是那些对于人类来说确实过时的平凡任务。”

日产是一系列汽车公司中最新一家强调人工智能如何改变美国人制造汽车的方式，包括提高初始质量和缩短开发时间。

但它是少数愿意公开谈论人工智能如何监视其工人的公司之一。

人工智能可以修复工人弯曲和扭曲的方式

负责该系统实施的日产工艺工程师、前安全工程师 Chi Amaechi 表示，坎顿装配厂的每项工作都有所谓的“黄金周期”。

黄金循环代表了执行任务的标准方式，包括安装车辆部件的顺序、所需的时间以及旨在减少重复性劳损的身体动作。

“它的作用是主动监测身体角度，”她在向《商业内幕》进行虚拟演示时说道。 “它基本上是识别你的关节，因此它可以识别一个人何时弯曲到超出安全要求的位置。”

该系统可以检测员工何时弯腰过度或长时间保持不安全的姿势，然后为工厂经理标记潜在风险。 主管和工程师可以使用该信息来指导工人、重新分配任务或重新设计工作站。

Amaechi 表示，该技术取代了耗时的手动观察，这种观察可能会不一致，因为员工在知道有人在观察时可能会改变自己的行为。

泰勒表示，日产最初评估该技术是为了提高制造效率并帮助培训新工人。 人体工程学的好处后来才显现出来。

“我们最初并不是在寻找这个，”他谈到安全应用程序时说道。 “这似乎表明，这是最大的胜利。”

泰勒说，这项技术也成为日产应对劳动力老龄化的一部分。

“我们的员工已经在工厂工作了 20 到 30 多年，他们想退休，”他补充道。 “你无法取代 20、30 年的专业知识。”

泰勒表示，员工很早就通过工厂安全委员会参与其中。 他和 Amaechi 表示，工人们最初担心这项技术可能会威胁到工作，但当日产将其作为安全和培训工具提供时，他们变得更加容易接受。 他们还描述了工人们欢迎使用该系统做出的改变的例子。

泰勒表示，总体而言，该技术为坎顿节省了约 3400 万美元的安全和健康相关费用。

该系统仅部署在广州。 泰勒表示，日产计划在那里完成其部署，然后将其扩展到该公司位于田纳西州士麦那的装配厂，并评估其动力总成工厂的应用。

一个大转变

日产汽车经历了艰难的几年，但它已显示出扭亏为盈的早期迹象。

2025 年 4 月，日产和本田放弃合并谈判后不久，伊万·埃斯皮诺萨 (Ivan Espinosa) 取代内田诚 (Makoto Uchida) 担任首席执行官。 埃斯皮诺萨随后推出了一项复苏计划，重点是裁员、降低制造能力和精简日产的运营。

坎顿的装配线受到了其中一些削减的影响：5月，该公司取消了在工厂生产电动汽车的 5 亿美元计划。

周一，日产公布了两年来首次季度净利润，这得益于成本削减以及美国和日本销售的强劲增长。 该汽车制造商表示，本季度其美国销量增长近 10%，并称自己是过去 10 个月增长最快的主流品牌。

该公司称自己为美国“增长最快的主流”汽车品牌（按销量计算）。
